```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(omopduckdb)
```

The OMOP CDM does not define everything a protocol needs. An area deprivation index, the rural-urban code of the home ZIP, the
median household income of the census tract, a site's own comorbidity score: none of these is a standard concept, so the OHDSI
tools (FeatureExtraction, PatientLevelPrediction, DeepPatientLevelPrediction) cannot see them.

A **study-design feature** is such a feature. `omopduckdb` ships a small framework, not a data set:

| You write | The package does |
|---|---|
| a `study_feature()` (or a built-in: `ruca_feature()`, `sdi_feature()`, `area_feature()`, `sql_feature()`, `custom_feature()`) | resolves the address in effect at admission once, computes every feature for the index stays, keeps the fitted state |
| a `feature_set()` you extend with `add_feature()` | writes the values as `measurement` rows under site-defined concepts and builds the FeatureExtraction covariate settings |
| the reference table (ACS income, RUCA, SDI) | never bundles it: you supply it, the package only does the join, the transform and the missingness handling |

The same API exists in Python (`omop_etl.study_features`), and the manifest and fitted state are interchangeable between the two.

## A small synthetic CDM

Six patients with a dated address history and one inpatient stay each. Everything below is synthetic.

```{r cdm}
db_path <- tempfile(fileext = ".duckdb")
build_schema(db_path)
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = db_path)

zips <- c("19104", "15213", "08101", "17821", "19104", "99999")   # 99999 is in no reference table
for (i in 1:6) {
  DBI::dbExecute(con, sprintf("INSERT INTO person (person_id, gender_concept_id, year_of_birth, race_concept_id, ethnicity_concept_id)
                               VALUES (%d, 8507, 1960, 0, 0)", i))
  DBI::dbExecute(con, sprintf("INSERT INTO visit_occurrence (visit_occurrence_id, person_id, visit_concept_id, visit_start_date,
                               visit_end_date, visit_type_concept_id) VALUES (%d, %d, 9201, DATE '2018-0%d-10', DATE '2018-0%d-14', 0)",
                              i, i, i, i))
}
DBI::dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE person_address_history (person_id BIGINT, location_id BIGINT, zip5 VARCHAR,
                      address_start DATE, address_end DATE, preferred VARCHAR)")
for (i in 1:6) DBI::dbExecute(con, sprintf("INSERT INTO person_address_history VALUES (%d, %d, '%s', DATE '2010-01-01', NULL, 'Y')", i, i, zips[i]))
```

The reference tables are plain data frames (or CSV paths). The column names are matched case-insensitively.

```{r tables}
ruca   <- data.frame(ZIPCODE = c("19104", "15213", "08101", "17821"), RUCA_CODE = c("1", "2.1", "4", "99"))
sdi    <- data.frame(ZCTA5_FIPS = c("19104", "15213", "08101", "17821"), SDI_score = c(95, 40, 10, 70))
income <- data.frame(zcta = c("19104", "15213", "08101", "17821"), median_income = c(31000, 88000, 61000, 54000))
sdi_cuts <- c(20, 45, 65, 85)      # the training cohort's fixed SDI cut points
```

## Build a feature set

A feature set is extended one feature at a time, so a study can start with geography and add features later.

```{r set}
fs <- feature_set() |>
  add_feature(ruca_feature(ruca)) |>
  add_feature(sdi_feature(sdi, cut_points = sdi_cuts))
fs
feature_set_columns(fs)
```

`area_feature()` turns *any* ZIP-keyed number into a feature. Median household income is right-skewed, so use `log1p`; a
`percentile` transform instead puts every site on the training distribution (see "Across sites" below).

```{r income}
add_feature(fs, area_feature("income", income, "median_income", transform = "log1p"))
feature_set_columns(fs)
```

## Compute for the index stays

`stays_from_cohort()` turns a cohort table into the index stays; here we use every inpatient visit (the default).

```{r compute}
wide <- compute_features(fs, con)
wide[order(wide$stay_id), ]
```

* The address is the one **in effect at admission** (the rule of `derive_geography_features()`), never a later one.
* A ZIP missing from a table gives `NA` and `income_missing = 1` (patient 6); turn the indicator off with
  `missing_indicator = FALSE` or fill with the training median using `impute = TRUE`.
* RUCA 99 ("not coded") lands in small town / rural as in the reference study; pass `code_99_missing = TRUE` to treat it as unknown.

## Make it visible to OHDSI tools

`write_feature_set()` stores each value as a `measurement` row dated the admission date, under a site-defined concept
(>= 2,000,000,000). SDI and RUCA keep the ids of `GEOGRAPHY_CONCEPT_IDS`, so earlier work stays compatible; everything else is
registered for you.

```{r write}
concepts <- write_feature_set(fs, con, wide)
format(vapply(concepts, function(x) as.numeric(x[[1]]), numeric(1)), scientific = FALSE)
cat(feature_set_extraction_r(fs, concepts))
```

`feature_set_covariate_settings(fs, concepts)` returns the same thing as a real FeatureExtraction object:

```{r fe, eval = requireNamespace("FeatureExtraction", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("DatabaseConnector", quietly = TRUE)}
DBI::dbExecute(con, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS cohort")
DBI::dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE cohort (cohort_definition_id INT, subject_id BIGINT, cohort_start_date DATE, cohort_end_date DATE)")
DBI::dbExecute(con, "INSERT INTO cohort SELECT 1, person_id, visit_start_date, visit_end_date FROM visit_occurrence")
DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

conn <- DatabaseConnector::connect(DatabaseConnector::createConnectionDetails(dbms = "duckdb", server = db_path))
cov <- FeatureExtraction::getDbCovariateData(
  connection = conn, cdmDatabaseSchema = "main", cohortTable = "cohort", cohortDatabaseSchema = "main",
  cohortIds = 1, rowIdField = "subject_id", aggregated = FALSE,
  covariateSettings = feature_set_covariate_settings(fs, concepts))
DatabaseConnector::disconnect(conn)
head(as.data.frame(cov$covariateRef)[, c("covariateId", "covariateName")])
```

From there the covariates feed PatientLevelPrediction exactly like any other FeatureExtraction output. `SQL`-defined or custom-R
features (below) take the same path.

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
if (DBI::dbIsValid(con)) DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
unlink(db_path)
```

## Your own feature

Three ways, from least to most code:

```{r own, eval = FALSE}
# 1. A SQL query over the OMOP tables, reading the view `_stays` (person_id, stay_id, admit_date)
prior_ed <- sql_feature("n_prior_ed", "
  SELECT s.stay_id, CAST(count(*) AS DOUBLE) AS n_prior_ed
  FROM _stays s JOIN visit_occurrence v
    ON v.person_id = s.person_id AND v.visit_concept_id = 9203 AND v.visit_start_date < s.admit_date
  GROUP BY 1", columns = "n_prior_ed")

# 2. Your own R function: fn(con, stays) -> stay_id + the numeric columns
frailty <- custom_feature("frailty", "frailty_index", function(con, stays) my_frailty_index(con, stays))

# 3. A complete study_feature() with fitted state, requirements and concept ids (see ?study_feature)
```

The contract is the author's: a feature may only use data dated before the index date (or during the stay when the protocol
says so). Nothing in the framework reads events after discharge.

## The same API in Python

These examples are illustrative and are not run when the package is built.

`omop_etl.study_features` is the Python twin of the R API described above. Names map one to one
(`add_feature` is `FeatureSet.add`, `compute_features` is `FeatureSet.compute`, `write_feature_set` is `FeatureSet.write`, ...), the
manifest format is the same, and fitted state moves freely between the languages: fit in Python, apply in R, or the other way.

### Build, compute, write

```python
import duckdb, pandas as pd
from omop_etl import FeatureSet, ruca_feature, sdi_feature, area_feature, stays_from_cohort

con = duckdb.connect("omop.duckdb")
fs = (FeatureSet()
      .add(ruca_feature("ruca_crosswalk.csv"))
      .add(sdi_feature("sdi.csv", cut_points=[20.8, 40.6, 60.4, 80.2]))      # the training cohort's fixed cuts
      .add(area_feature("income", "acs_b19013.csv", "median_income", transform="log1p")))

stays = stays_from_cohort(con, "cohort")             # person_id, stay_id, admit_date (cohort order)
wide = fs.compute(con, stays)                        # one row per stay, input order
concepts = fs.write(con, wide)                       # measurement rows under site-defined concepts
print(fs.feature_extraction_r(concepts))             # the FeatureExtraction covariate settings, as R code
```

`fs.compute` returns the fitted state in `wide.attrs["feature_state"]` and the manifest in `wide.attrs["feature_provenance"]`.

### Fit once, apply everywhere

```python
fs_train = FeatureSet([sdi_feature("sdi.csv"),
                       area_feature("income", "acs_b19013.csv", "median_income", transform="percentile", impute=True)])
fs_train.compute(con_train, stays_train, fit=True)       # learns cut points, percentile grid, median fill
fs_train.export_manifest("study_features.json")

fs_site = FeatureSet([sdi_feature("sdi.csv"),
                      area_feature("income", "acs_b19013.csv", "median_income", transform="percentile", impute=True)])
fs_site.load_state("study_features.json")                # no local fitting; without it the transforms raise
site = fs_site.compute(con_site, stays_site)
```

### Your own features in Python

```python
from omop_etl import sql_feature, custom_feature

prior_ed = sql_feature("n_prior_ed", """
    SELECT s.stay_id, count(*)::DOUBLE AS n_prior_ed
    FROM _stays s JOIN visit_occurrence v
      ON v.person_id = s.person_id AND v.visit_concept_id = 9203 AND v.visit_start_date < s.admit_date
    GROUP BY 1""", ["n_prior_ed"])

frailty = custom_feature("frailty", ["frailty_index"], lambda con, stays: my_frailty(con, stays))
fs.add(prior_ed).add(frailty)
```

A package or a study can also register a whole kind of feature and name lists of them:

```python
from omop_etl.study_features import register_feature_factory, FEATURE_LISTS, feature_list

register_feature_factory("frailty", frailty_factory)
FEATURE_LISTS["my_protocol"] = ("ruca", "sdi", "frailty")
fs = feature_list("my_protocol", ruca={"crosswalk": ...}, sdi={"table": ..., "cut_points": cuts}, frailty={...})
```

### Deep-learning datasets

Area features are static, so they go to the dense block of `extract_multimodal_deep_dataset()`. Use `transform="percentile"` or
`"zscore"` with *training* state, keep `<name>_missing`, and avoid raw dollars: a high-capacity sequence model can otherwise use the
income scale to recognise the site (see "Across sites" below).

## Across sites: fitted state, manifests and deep models

A model that uses an area-level feature must compute it **the same way at every site**. Two things go wrong silently:

1. **Quantile drift.** Cutting SDI into quintiles at the *local* quantiles moves patients between quintiles whenever a site's
   deprivation distribution differs from training.
2. **Scale drift.** Raw income in dollars differs by an order of magnitude between an urban and a rural network. A high-capacity model
   can use it to recognise the site instead of learning disease risk.

The framework therefore separates *fitting* from *applying*. A transform that learns from data (SDI cut points, a percentile grid,
a mean and sd, an imputation median) is fitted **once, on the training sites, with `fit = TRUE`**, stored as the feature's *state*,
shipped in a manifest, and reused unchanged elsewhere. Without state a learned transform refuses to run.

### Two synthetic sites

```{r sites}
make_site <- function(zips, year = 2018) {
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".duckdb")
  build_schema(path)
  con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = path)
  DBI::dbExecute(con, "CREATE TABLE person_address_history (person_id BIGINT, location_id BIGINT, zip5 VARCHAR,
                        address_start DATE, address_end DATE, preferred VARCHAR)")
  for (i in seq_along(zips)) {
    DBI::dbExecute(con, sprintf("INSERT INTO person (person_id, gender_concept_id, year_of_birth, race_concept_id, ethnicity_concept_id)
                                 VALUES (%d, 8507, 1960, 0, 0)", i))
    DBI::dbExecute(con, sprintf("INSERT INTO visit_occurrence (visit_occurrence_id, person_id, visit_concept_id, visit_start_date,
                                 visit_end_date, visit_type_concept_id) VALUES (%d, %d, 9201, DATE '%d-03-01', DATE '%d-03-04', 0)",
                                i, i, year, year))
    DBI::dbExecute(con, sprintf("INSERT INTO person_address_history VALUES (%d, %d, '%s', DATE '2000-01-01', NULL, 'Y')", i, i, zips[i]))
  }
  list(con = con, path = path)
}

# the reference tables are national, so both sites use the same ones
area <- data.frame(zcta = sprintf("%05d", 10000 + 0:59),
                   sdi = seq(5, 100, length.out = 60),
                   income = seq(24000, 190000, length.out = 60))

training <- make_site(area$zcta)                # a large mixed network: the whole range
new_site <- make_site(area$zcta[41:60])         # a smaller network drawn from the deprived, low-income end
```

### Fit on the training site

```{r fit}
build_set <- function() {
  feature_set(
    sdi_feature(area[, c("zcta", "sdi")]),                                              # no cut points yet
    area_feature("income", area[, c("zcta", "income")], "income", transform = "percentile", impute = TRUE))
}
fs_train <- build_set()
train <- compute_features(fs_train, training$con, fit = TRUE)

st <- feature_set_state(fs_train)
st$sdi$cut_points
length(st$income$percentile_grid)
```

`fit` can also name features (`fit = "income"`), so one feature can be refit without touching the others.

### Ship the manifest with the model

```{r manifest}
manifest <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
export_feature_manifest(fs_train, manifest)
substr(paste(readLines(manifest, n = 22), collapse = "\n"), 1, 520)
```

The manifest records every feature's columns, required tables, parameters, fitted state and the concept ids. It contains nothing
about patients.

### Apply at the new site

```{r apply}
fs_new <- build_set()
load_feature_state(fs_new, manifest)               # also accepts a manifest written by Python
new <- compute_features(fs_new, new_site$con)

# the same SDI score gets the same quintile at both sites
table(train$sdi_quintile)
table(new$sdi_quintile)

# income is a position in the *training* distribution, so it is comparable
range(train$income); range(new$income)
```

The new site sits in the top two SDI quintiles and the upper third of the *training* income distribution, as it should. Local quantiles
would have spread it over all five quintiles and hidden exactly the difference the model needs to see.

Skip the state and the learned transforms refuse:

```{r refuse, error = TRUE}
compute_features(build_set(), new_site$con)
```

### Deep models

`extract_multimodal_deep_dataset()` keeps temporal sequence tokens apart from static covariates (`dense_covariates`). Area features
are static, so they belong in the dense block, and three rules follow from the above:

* **Scale them.** Dollars would dominate token embeddings. Use `percentile` or `zscore` with *training* state, never the
  statistics of the batch or the site.
* **Prefer relative scales across sites.** A percentile of the national distribution transports; raw income can act as a site
  identifier.
* **Keep the missing indicator.** `<name>_missing` lets the network tell "unmapped ZIP" from "average ZIP" after imputation.

```{r deep, eval = FALSE}
wide <- compute_features(fs_new, new_site$con, stays_from_cohort(new_site$con, "cohort"))
# merge on visit_occurrence_id, then give the numeric columns to the dense block
```

### Sharing concept ids

Concept ids for registered features are per database. For a consortium, pin them with a shared registry so every site writes the same
ids:

```{r registry, eval = FALSE}
export_custom_concept_registry(con_lead, "custom_concepts.json")      # lead site
write_feature_set(fs, con, wide, registry = "custom_concepts.json")   # every other site
check_custom_concepts(con, "custom_concepts.json")                    # catches a mismatch before anything is written
```

```{r cleanup-sites, include = FALSE}
for (s in list(training, new_site)) { DBI::dbDisconnect(s$con, shutdown = TRUE); unlink(s$path) }
unlink(manifest)
```
